summary: Piscataquis County, ME: 36-foot steel lookout, staffed in 1940, restoration stalled after 2013 stabilization, removed 2017.

facts.design: 36-foot steel lookout tower (steel hauled for it in 1926; height given as 36 feet in 1935)
facts.status_note: Removed in 2017, according to the FFLA Maine chapter's 2017 tower survey; no source describes what remains at the site

events.note: Maine Forest Service panoramic map centered on a fire tower in Township 1, Range 12
Steel hauled for a new 36-foot steel lookout tower; completion date not confirmed in the sources read
Lewiston Daily Sun item (May 25, 1935) gave the tower height as 36 feet
Linwood Rideout worked six weeks in the lookout for the Maine State Forest Commission (reported September 11, 1940)
Friends of Wadleigh Mountain formed to pursue restoration; proposal presented to the state
Two fall maintenance trips were made up the mountain as a stabilization effort; it was weather tight for winter 2013/2014. The report calls this stabilization, not restoration
State had budgeted some funds for structural evaluations; no decision on the proposal
State agreed to perform a structural analysis in 2016 as a prerequisite to any restoration plans
Restoration project officially on hold until the state completes its structural analysis
Lookout removed (FFLA Maine chapter 2017 tower survey); FFLA worked with Parks and Lands to obtain a 12-foot ladder section for use at the Squaw Mountain tower

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 2013 'restored' event overstates the source: the 2013 report calls two trips a stabilization effort, and the 2014 to 2016 reports show the restoration still awaiting state approval or analysis. Recorded here as 'other'.

notes_for_editor: Build history is unclear: a 1919 map shows a fire tower, and 1926 steel-tower work is the first documented construction. The sources do not say whether the 1926 tower replaced the 1919 one, so the story does not claim it. The record's 2013 'restored' event should read as stabilization, not restoration. No source describes the site today or public access. FFLA Facebook posts about the 2017 removal could not be read, so they are not used.
